title: Ramen Profitable: why covering founders' living expenses buys time and leverage
summary: Paul Graham defines ramen profitability as a startup making just enough to pay the founders' living expenses. It buys time and independence from investors, and it is not the destination. He lists four advantages (better terms, investor appeal, morale, no fundraising distraction) and warns about sliding into consulting.

principles.text: Ramen profitability means covering founders' living expenses; its value is buying time, not signaling success.
principles.quote: Ramen profitable means a startup makes just enough to pay the founders' living expenses.

principles.text: Once you're ramen profitable you stop being at the mercy of investors and get better terms.
principles.quote: The main significance of this type of profitability is that you're no longer at the mercy of investors.

principles.text: Even small profitability reassures investors: someone pays you, you're serious about users, and you keep costs low.
principles.quote: If you're already profitable, on however small a scale, it shows that (a) you can get at least someone to pay you, (b) you're serious about building things people want, and (c) you're disciplined enough to keep expenses low.

principles.text: Covering your own expenses lifts morale by making survival the default, and responsibility is what makes startups hard.
principles.quote: Now survival is the default, instead of dying.

principles.text: Fundraising wrecks productivity because it takes over the one urgent problem you think about constantly.
principles.quote: Raising money is terribly distracting. You're lucky if your productivity is a third of what it was before.

principles.text: Beware drifting into consulting: startups must make a product that scales, and ramen profitability is only a trick for not dying.
principles.quote: A startup's destination is to grow really big; ramen profitability is a trick for not dying en route.
